episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: So the key was the Apple partnership.
If they had launched this in a Home Depot, just on the shelf next to all the other Philips bulbs, I just think it would have really struggled.
But because they were able to partner with Apple, get into the Apple stores, they were reaching the correct audience, to your point.
They were reaching people that were willing to try this out.
And then that gave them the runway to then be able to develop a product that everyone could use.
Because originally it was also iPhone only, obviously, to begin with.
So I think that was a really key being in the Apple stores.
But he said they because it was incredibly expensive to manufacture these bulbs.
He said they lost money on every single bulb they sold at the beginning.
Yeah.
It was no profit margin because this technology was so new and they had put so much resources and engineering into it.
At 60 bucks a bulb, they're losing money.
60 a bulb, they were losing money.
Wow.
And he said, you know, and obviously that was their biggest fear is that the price was going to cause people to not buy this.
But so originally they only made, he didn't give me a number, but the first run was very constrained because they really weren't sure.
They knew they had a great product.
They just didn't know that they were going to be able to communicate that to the target audience.
And the Apple store really ended up being key to that.
I remember writing at the time about how all the retailers were struggling so bad trying to figure out how to market smart home products.
And they all were just terrible at it.

Apple understood retail and considered the fact that most of the people that walk into that store are going in there with the mentality that I'm going to spend more for something in this store than I would pretty much anywhere else.
Right.
They're buying Apple products.
They are already paying an Apple tax.
Right.
